title.en: The Ramayana of Valmiki: Rama's Exile, Sita's Abduction, and the War of Lanka
title.zh: 蟻垤《羅摩衍那》：羅摩流放、悉多被擄與楞伽之戰

texts.period: Oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (critical edition, Oriental Institute Baroda, 1960-75); principal mediaeval mss numerous (e.g. Newari, Devanagari traditions)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg (Griffith translation, 1870-74) / Princeton University Press (critical translation: Goldman)
source.work: Ramayana of Valmiki, kandas I-VII; trans. R. T. H. Griffith (public domain); The Ramayana of Valmiki, gen. ed. Robert P. Goldman (Princeton)

texts.license: Public domain (Griffith translation 1870-74); passages below mostly labeled paraphrases of the Sanskrit

summary.en: Prince Rama of Ayodhya is exiled fourteen years by a rival queen's boon; his wife Sita is abducted by the ten-headed Ravana to Lanka; with monkey allies and Hanuman's leap, Rama builds a bridge, destroys Ravana, and returns to rule the ideal kingdom — the charter epic of dharma-king and devoted wife, retold at Ramanavami and Dashehra.
summary.zh: 阿逾陀王子羅摩遭後母之詛流放十四載；妻悉多為十首羅波那擄至楞伽；羅摩得神猴哈奴曼相助，跨海建橋、誅羅波那，攜妻歸國，行理想之治——為印度『達摩之王』與『貞婦』之根本史詩，羅摩誕辰節與十勝節年年重述。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: the Ramayana is read ritually (Ramanavami, Ramcaritmanas recitation). Classified 'myth' rather than 'religious' per the README's interpretive split (epic literature rather than sruti/smrti scripture); reasoning recorded here.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Ayodhya Kanda 34-35: Kaikeyi demands her two boons — that Bharata be consecrated heir, and Rama be banished to the forest for fourteen years wearing bark garments. Rama accepts without protest: 'For father's promise, and for dharma, I go to Dandaka.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Ayodhya Kanda 34-35; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Sundara Kanda 21-22: Sita, seated under the Ashoka tree, refuses Ravana's offer of queenship, placing a blade of grass between them; Hanuman reveals himself, gives Rama's ring, and offers to carry her back — she refuses to touch another male, bidding Rama come for her. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sundara Kanda 21-22; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: R. T. H. Griffith, The Ramayan of Valmiki, 5 vols., Benares, 1870-74 (public domain); modern critical translation: Robert P. Goldman et al., The Ramayana of Valmiki, 7 vols., Princeton University Press, 1984-2017

narrative.en:
The poem's framing 'adi' (first) kanda announces its own composition: Valmiki asks Narada, 'Who in this world today is virtuous, mighty, truthful, and self-controlled?' — the answer, Rama, prince of Kosala, launches 24,000 slokas of the first fully developed Sanskrit kavya.

BALA KANDA. King Dasharatha of Ayodhya, childless, performs the putrakamesti sacrifice; a divine being rises from the fire and gives the king golden rice to divide among his three queens. Four sons are born: Rama of Kausalya, Bharata of Kaikeyi, Lakshmana and Shatrughna of Sumitra — partial incarnations of Vishnu, come at the gods' request (plagued by Ravana) to destroy the ten-headed king of Lanka. The seer Vishvamitra leads the adolescent Rama and Lakshmana into the forest: Rama kills the ogress Tataka (a yakshi-turned-rakshasi whose death must come from a man, not a god), frees the sage's fire-sacrifices from rakshasa raiders, and is given celestial weapons. On the return, at Mithila, Rama breaks — with a bow-string's sound no less than his rivals can barely lift — Shiva's bow at Janaka's contest, and weds the foundling-princess Sita ('found in the furrow', sita 'furrow'), whose swayamvara has defeated every demon king. The four brothers marry the four brides; Vishvamitra tells Rama the gods' distress at Ravana's sway.

AYODHYA KANDA. Aging Dasharatha resolves to consecrate Rama heir-apparent. On the eve of the ceremony, the hunchbacked maid Manthara persuades Queen Kaikeyi to cash in two boons Dasharatha granted long ago for nursing him: that Bharata be consecrated instead, and Rama be exiled to the forest for fourteen years in bark garments. Kaikeyi complies; Dasharatha collapses in grief. Rama, told, accepts without a word of protest — 'not for father's command, but for truth and for dharma' — and Sita insists on following ('a father, a mother, a brother, a son may be banished; a wife follows her husband wherever he goes'); Lakshmana walks before them in anger. The three cross the Ganga (aided by Guha, chief of the boatmen) to Chitrakuta; Dasharatha dies grieving the broken bond; Bharata, refusing the throne his mother engineered, tracks Rama to Chitrakuta and begs him to return. Rama holds to the vow: fourteen years, not a day less. Bharata returns with Rama's golden sandals (paduka), places them on the throne at Nandigrama, and rules from the village gate as regent, a mark of ideal ministerial dharma.

ARANYA KANDA. The trio settles at Panchavati in Dandaka; the rakshasi Surpanakha, sister of Ravana, approaches Rama, then Lakshmana, and is mutilated — nose and ears cut — when she attacks Sita; her brothers Khara and Dushana attack with 14,000 rakshasas and are destroyed by Rama alone. Surpanakha goads Ravana: the ten-headed, twenty-armed king of Lanka sends the sorcerer Maricha as a golden deer. Sita, charmed, demands it; the dying Maricha cries Lakshmana's name in Rama's voice; Sita, believing Rama slain, orders Lakshmana to help, and — in this telling — the prince is goaded into leaving her (the famous 'Lakshmana-line' with which later tellings arm Sita is absent from Valmiki). Ravana, disguised as an ascetic, crosses the hut's boundary, seizes Sita and her hut together, and drives her skyward; the vulture Jatayus, Dasharatha's old friend, fights him aloft and is mortally wounded, living just long enough to tell Rama who took her. Dying, Rama performs Jatayus' last rites.

KISHKINDHA KANDA. Rama and Lakshmana reach Lake Pampa; the monkey Hanuman, son of the wind-god, in disguise brings them to Sugriva, the exiled monkey king. A friendship pact is made: Rama kills Vali (Sugriva's brother and usurper) with a single hidden arrow in their duel — an act debated ever since for its ethics; the rainy season passes with Rama's grief and Hanuman's counsel; then four monkey armies are dispatched to the world's quarters. In the south, the vulture Sampati (Jatayus' brother) confirms Sita's location: Lanka, across the sea.

SUNDARA KANDA ('the beautiful one', named for Sita's island ordeal). Hanuman, son of the wind, leaps across a hundred yojanas of ocean, evading the snake-mother Surasa and the demoness Sinhika, and lands at Lanka by night. In the Ashoka grove he finds Sita, surrounded by rakshasi guards and Ravana's ultimatum; she has placed a blade of grass between them, and refused the term of one year before Ravana kills her. Hanuman reveals himself, offers to carry her back; she refuses to be touched by another male and gives Rama her chudamani gem. Hanuman destroys the grove and the escort, lets himself be captured (killing Ravana's son Aksha in the duel), delivers Rama's warning before Ravana's court — with Vibhishana's dissent — and is sent out with his tail afire; he burns the golden city, spares the Ashoka grove, and leaps home.

YUDDHA KANDA. Rama's host marches to the sea; Ravana's brother Vibhishana defects, is sheltered against the council's qualms, and is later consecrated king. The ocean-god advises Nala the monkey-builder; the Nala Setu bridge is built of stones that float. The war rages for days: Kumbhakarna, roused from his six-month sleep, devours armies until Rama's arrows sever his head; Indrajit's serpent-arrows bind Rama and Lakshmana until Garuda frees them; Indrajit's illusory Sita-decapitation nearly breaks the army's heart; Vibhishana's counsel and Lakshmana's Indra-astra kill Indrajit in the Nikumbhila rite. Finally Rama faces Ravana: each arrow-match fails, until Rama invokes the Brahmastra, slaying the ten heads; Vibhishana mourns the brother he served, and Sita is brought out from the grove. 'My heart is with Rama', she says; but Rama, before the army, renounces her — she has lived in another man's house. Sita demands the fire-pyre (agni-pariksha): Agni himself bears her out unharmed — 'I know the purity of my own heart; the shadow-Sita I carried away was illusion'. The gods descend; Indra restores Rama's slain monkey army, and Rama is consecrated in Lanka. The pushpaka vimana (Ravana's flying palace) carries all to Ayodhya: Bharata, fourteen years of regency fulfilled, gives up the throne; Rama rules the ideal kingdom (rama-rajya), where 'no widow mourns, no disease, no thieves' — the aition of Divali's lamps.

UTTARA KANDA (in the critical edition, an appendix with debated status). Rumors circulate that the king accepted a woman who lived in Ravana's house; Rama banishes the pregnant Sita to Valmiki's ashrama, where she bears twins Lava and Kusha, whom the poet raises and teaches to sing the Ramayana itself — the self-referential moment when the epic is first recited in Rama's court. Sita, summoned, again proves herself: 'If I have never thought of any but Rama, let Earth receive me'; the earth opens, Bhudevi receives her on a golden throne, and Rama rules alone until he enters the Sarayu river, resuming his form as Vishnu.

FUNCTIONS. The Ramayana is the charter narrative of Hindu kingship (rama-rajya as political ideal), of pativrata wifely dharma (Sita), of filial obedience (Rama, Bharata, Lakshmana), and of devotion (bhakti) to Vishnu in the form of Rama; it is ritually recited at Ramanavami (Rama's birth), and Ravana's effigies burn at Vijayadashami (Dashehra); Tulsidas' Ramcaritmanas recitation structures north Indian devotional life; and Hanuman's cult (Tuesdays, Hanuman Jayanti) hangs on his Sundara Kanda feats.
narrative.zh: 阿逾陀王十車王求子得四子，羅摩為毘濕奴化身。尊者維什瓦米陀攜二王子誅羅剎，至彌提羅折濕婆神弓，娶犁溝所出之悉多。老王欲立羅摩，後妃凱凱伊受駝背婢慫恿索二諾：立婆羅多、放羅摩十四年。羅摩攜悉多與弟羅什曼那入林；羅剎女首哩薄那迦受辱，慫恿兄羅波那遣摩哩遮化金鹿誘王，化作苦行者擄走悉多；神鷲闍吒優私力戰而死。羅摩結盟神猴須羯哩婆，一箭誅猴王婆黎；哈奴曼躍海覓妻，火燒楞伽城。羅摩於海上建那羅橋，大戰：誅巨猿俱姆伽爾那、妖術師因陀羅耆，終以梵箭破十首之頸；維毗沙那受封。悉多過火驗，火神親護而出，證其貞潔。飛車歸國，婆羅多還政，羅摩行『羅摩之治』。後篇：羅摩放逐有孕之悉多至蟻垤仙人林中，生二子；二子誦此史詩於王廷；悉多再驗，呼大地開口受之；羅摩入薩羅逾河復毗濕奴之身。功能：君權典範、貞婦達摩、孝悌之義、羅摩誕辰與十勝節之禮儀重述。

functions: Charter of ideal kingship (rama-rajya) and ministerial dharma (Bharata's regency)
Pativrata ideal: Sita's trial as the normative narrative of wifely constancy
Ritual calendar: Ramanavami recitation, Vijayadashami burning of Ravana effigies, Divali lamps
Bhakti charter: Rama as Vishnu's avatar; Hanuman's cult founded on the Sundara Kanda

variants.name: Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas
variants.summary: The vernacular retelling that displaced Valmiki in north Indian recitation; adds the lakshmana-rekha line around Sita's hut and shifts emphasis to Rama's divinity (bhakti) over kingship ethics.

variants.name: Kampan's Iramavataram (Tamil, 12th c. CE)
variants.summary: Tamil retelling with far more developed Rama-devotion (Rama as Vishnu from the start), rich descriptive style, and local motifs (Sita's birth is as a goddess); the canonical South Indian version, ritually recited in Tamil temples.

variants.name: Paumacariya of Vimalasuri (Jain, c. 3rd-5th c. CE)
variants.summary: Jain retelling in which Ravana is a tragic, noble rakshasa-king (killed for the Jain vow-breaking of his son), Lakshmana (not Rama) kills him, and Rama is a Jain hero of the 8th bhavya-line — the ideology reworked through ahimsa and karma.

variants.name: Dasaratha Jataka (Buddhist, Pali)
variants.summary: A Buddhist parable version: Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana are exiled to the Himalayas; Ravana never abducts Sita; Sita remains Rama's sister (in this telling) and the story ends in reconciliation — no Lanka, no war, a didactic tale of non-attachment.

variants.name: Thai Ramakien and Khmer Reamker
variants.text_tradition: Thai dance-drama (Rattanakosin period); Khmer classical ballet
variants.summary: Southeast Asian court adaptations: Rama as an incarnation of Vishnu legitimates the king (Bangkok's dynasty takes the name Rama); the monkey armies are localized and the war becomes national pageant (khon masked dance).

variants.name: Kakawin Ramayana (Old Javanese)
variants.text_tradition: Old Javanese kavya, c. 9th-10th c. CE
variants.summary: Javanese court version integrating the epic with local architecture (Prambanan reliefs) and poetic conventions; ancestor of Balinese and Javanese wayang tellings.

variants.name: 'Three Hundred Ramayanas' corpus
variants.text_tradition: A. K. Ramanujan's survey (1991) of told traditions
variants.summary: Ramanujan's famous essay catalogues dozens of tellings — Sanskrit, Tamil, Thai, Javanese, Kannada, folk — across languages and media; the corpus is the standard scholarly frame for the tradition's variance.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The Ramayana is ritually recited and politically contested in contemporary India (e.g. court debates over Sita's trial narratives). Quote from public-domain or critical translations; attribute kanda and sarga; note which recension is quoted (critical edition vs. vulgar text differs at the Uttara Kanda); avoid framing the agni-pariksha as fact — it is narrated as divine test and debated in living practice.

title.en: The Churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra-manthana)

region.en: Cosmic ocean (symbolic pin at Varanasi ghats, Ganges)
region.zh: 宇宙之海（象徵性定位於恆河瓦拉納西河壇）

texts.period: Mahabharata Adi Parva (composition layers c. 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE; critical edition BORI, Poona); Purana versions c. 4th-10th c. CE

source.archive: Project Gutenberg (Mahabharata translations) / University of Chicago Press (van Buitenen)
source.work: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Astika Upaparva 18-34), trans. J. A. B. van Buitenen (Chicago, 1973)

texts.license: Cuneiform-free; van Buitenen translation quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Devas and Asuras, half-brothers, churn the cosmic ocean with the serpent Vasuki and Mount Mandara, supported by the tortoise Kurma; from the ocean come treasures, Lakshmi, and the amrita of immortality; Vishnu as the enchantress Mohini distributes it only to the gods, who thereby defeat death and their cousins.
summary.zh: 天神與阿修羅本為半血兄弟，以蛇王伐蘇基為繩、曼陀羅山為杵攪拌乳海，毗濕奴化巨龜托山；海中湧出寶物、吉祥天女與不死甘露；毗濕奴化身舞女摩希尼分甘露獨予天神，天神遂得不死、逐退阿修羅。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: the narrative is depicted in temple art and retold at festivals (e.g. Sharad Purnima, Lakshmi worship). Classified 'myth' per the README's interpretive split.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Adi Parva 18-19 (Astika Upaparva): Vishnu advises the gods, weakened by Durvasas' curse and war, to make peace with the Asuras and churn the ocean of milk for the amrita; Mandara is used as the churning-stick, the serpent Vasuki as the cord, and Vishnu, as the great tortoise, supports the mountain on his back. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Adi Parva 18-19 (Astika Upaparva); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Adi Parva 27-34: From the ocean rise Surabhi the cow of plenty, the Apsarases, Airavata, Ucchaihsravas, the Kaustubha gem, Parijata, the Moon, Lakshmi, Varuni, and finally Dhanvantari with the white amrita-vessel; the Asuras seize it, and Vishnu as Mohini allots it to the gods alone. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Adi Parva 27-34; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: J. A. B. van Buitenen, The Mahabharata, vol. 1, University of Chicago Press, 1973; alternate: Kisari Mohan Ganguli's public-domain translation (1883-96)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: A CURSE AND A PLAN. The Mahabharata's frame-story places the churning in the Astika section, told to protect a serpent-sacrifice. In the Purana versions, the sage Durvasas curses Indra (a garland crushed by his elephant): the king of the gods loses his fortune, and the Asuras, led by Bali, defeat the devas in war. The gods go to Brahma, then to Vishnu, who gives them the strategy: churn the ocean of milk (kshira-sagara) for the amrita, the nectar of immortality — but only in alliance with their enemies the Asuras, and with the agreement that the nectar will then be shared.

THE CHURNING. Mount Mandara is uprooted as the churning-stick; the serpent-king Vasuki (Ananta-Shesha in some tellings) offers himself as the churning-rope, wound around the mountain; the devas take the tail, the asuras the head (the asuras' position poisons them with Vasuki's venomous breath). The mountain sinks into the soft ocean-bed; Vishnu, in the form of the great tortoise Kurma (his second avatar), dives beneath and bears the mountain on his back. Brahma steadies the peak from above. And so, in the world's greatest tug-of-war, the brothers churn: 'as men churn with a cord', the mountain revolves 'with a great sound like thunder', the forest beasts fall from its slopes, the trees catch fire and the ocean froths. (In the Purana retellings, the churning's first product is the poison halahala/kalakuta, which threatens the three worlds and is drunk by Shiva, whose throat turns blue — Nilakantha, 'blue-throat'; the Mahabharata version has no poison and no Shiva.)

THE EMERGENCE. One by one, treasures rise from the milk ocean: Surabhi, the cow of plenty; Ucchaihsravas, the seven-headed horse of the sun; Airavata, the white elephant; the Kaustubha gem (Vishnu takes it for his breast); the Parijata tree; Apsarases, celestial dancers; Varuni, goddess of wine; Chandra, the Moon; then Lakshmi, goddess of fortune, who chooses Vishnu and garlands him — the aition of her marriage to Vishnu and of Sharad Purnima worship. Last rises Dhanvantari, physician of the gods, holding the white pot (kalasha) of amrita.

MOHINI AND THE END. The Asuras seize the pot; the devas panic; Vishnu resolves the impasse with his feminine illusion, Mohini ('the Enchantress'), the only female avatar in the canonical avatar-lists. Beautiful and unrecognizable, she offers to distribute the nectar 'fairly' and seats devas and asuras in two facing rows; she pours the amrita only into the devas' cups, deflecting the asuras with charm and with the promise of another round. (In the Purana tellings, the asura Svarbhanu disguises himself as a deva, drinks, and is decapitated mid-swallow by the sun and moon; his immortal head becomes Rahu, his body Ketu, the eclipse-demons.) The devas, immortal and restored, drive the asuras underground and to the sea; Vishnu hands the empty pot to Indra. The churned ocean, in some tellings, remains the cosmic treasury from which wealth continually arises.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative is the theology of the yajna: churning (manthana) is sacrificial labor, the ocean the ritual field, the pot the offering-vessel — the cosmos is enriched by brothers-in-conflict cooperating under a supervising god. It is the origin-story of Lakshmi's marriage, of the Kurma and (in Purana versions) the Shiva Nilakantha avatar-episodes, of Dhanvantari and Ayurveda, of Rahu-Ketu, and of Amrita's hieroglyph of immortality-in-community; its imagery structures Angkor Wat's third-gallery bas-relief (92 asuras, 88 devas pulling the naga Vasuki), Bangkok's Suvarnabhumi airport sculpture, and countless temple friezes across South and Southeast Asia.
narrative.zh: 仙人達爾瓦沙之詛令天神失運，阿修羅王巴利戰勝；毗濕奴授策：與阿修羅合盟，攪乳海取不死甘露。以曼陀羅山為杵、蛇王伐蘇基為繩，天神執尾、阿修羅執首，山沉海床，毗濕奴化身巨龜俱利摩托之，梵天自上扶正。攪動之初（往世書版）先出劇毒卡拉庫塔，濕婆一飲而盡，喉成青色，號『青頸』。繼而乳牛須羅毗、七頭神馬、白象艾羅婆多、寶石考斯圖巴、如意樹、飛天、酒神女伐魯尼、月亮相繼湧現；吉祥天女擇毗濕奴而冠之；末出醫神檀文陀梨，手捧白色甘露瓶。阿修羅奪瓶，毗濕奴化身摩希尼分配甘露，獨予天神（往世書版：偽裝之阿修羅斯伐爾巴努中途斬首，其首成日蝕之羅睺）。天神得不死，逐阿修羅入地，因陀羅復位。功能：祭祀之喻、吉祥天女婚配之源、醫神與阿育吠陀之始、日月蝕之神話釋義；吳哥窟迴廊浮雕即此景。

functions: Theology of sacrifice: churning as yajna, cosmos enriched by ritual labor
Origin narrative of Lakshmi's marriage and Sharad Purnima / Lakshmi worship
Aition of Dhanvantari and Ayurveda; of Rahu-Ketu as eclipse demons (Purana versions)
Pan-Asian visual iconography (Angkor Wat third gallery; Thai and Khmer royal symbolism)

variants.name: Mahabharata version (Adi Parva 18-34)
variants.summary: The oldest continuous telling: no poison episode and no Shiva; Vishnu (as Kurma and as Mohini) is the sole divine strategist; the frame serves the serpent-sacrifice story of Astika; Lakshmi's garland-choice is retained.

variants.name: Vishnu Purana and Bhagavata Purana versions
variants.summary: Add the halahala poison and Shiva Nilakantha (Bhagavata 8.7); introduce Rahu/Svarbhanu's decapitation (Vishnu Purana 4.9); elaborate Lakshmi's emergence and the sixty-four yoginis. The versions recited in temple worship today.

variants.name: Angkor Wat bas-relief (12th c. CE, Khmer)
variants.text_tradition: Khmer temple art, Gallery III, south wing
variants.summary: Monumental stone rendering: 92 asuras and 88 devas pull the naga Vasuki, Vishnu presides at the mountain's summit; a royal Khmer theology of cosmic order that makes the churning the visual charter of the temple-state.

variants.name: Thai Samudra-manthan iconography
variants.text_tradition: Thai royal art (Suvarnabhumi Airport installation; royal barge figureheads)
variants.summary: The churning becomes a royal emblem of legitimation — Rama-linked kingship imagery — with Vishnu centered and devas/asuras symmetrically ranked; adopted into court ritual and modern state symbolism.
